summary: Describes where and how the Label Distribution Protocol is meant to be used in MPLS networks. It explains the situations LDP suits, rather than defining new protocol rules. It is informational.

eli5.summary: This is a guide that says when it makes sense to use a particular tool for sharing tags between routers.

subtitle: A short guide to when label distribution with LDP is the right tool for MPLS networks.

tldr.problem: In MPLS, two Label Switching Routers must agree on what each label means. A label distribution protocol is how they tell each other.
tldr.mechanism: This memo describes where LDP fits. LDP sets up sessions over TCP, distributes labels for normally routed paths, and offers several modes to suit networks where labels are scarce or plentiful.
tldr.outcome: It recommends LDP for devices that do MPLS forwarding along normally routed paths, and leaves explicitly routed traffic engineering to CR-LDP or RSVP-TE.

facts.label: Requirement level
facts.value: Recommended for normally routed MPLS forwarding

today: RFC 3037 is an Informational memo and the metadata lists no replacement or update. It describes LDP as specified in RFC 3036.

sections.title: Where LDP Fits
sections.content:
MPLS forwards packets using short, fixed-length labels. Two Label Switching Routers (LSRs) must agree on what a label means, and a label distribution protocol is the set of procedures by which one LSR tells another about the bindings it has made.

The MPLS architecture allows more than one such method. This memo covers the Label Distribution Protocol (LDP), a protocol designed to support MPLS forwarding along normally routed paths chosen by destination-based routing protocols. This is sometimes called MPLS hop-by-hop forwarding.
sections.eli5: Routers need to agree on what each tag means. LDP is one way for them to tell each other, and this note explains when to use it.

sections.title: Where LDP Is Useful
sections.content:
The memo lists several settings where LDP suits the job:

  • With an IP routing plane and software to program switch cross-connect tables, LDP can run IP over a network of ATM or Frame Relay switches without an overlay or ATM-specific or Frame Relay-specific addressing or routing.
  • Efficient hop-by-hop routed tunnels, such as MPLS-based VPN architectures and tunneling between BGP border routers.
  • Paths that cross nodes which do not all support a common piggybacked approach to distributing labels, because LDP does not rely on specific routing protocols at every hop.

LDP also has a mechanism for extending it to MPLS features beyond best effort hop-by-hop forwarding.
sections.eli5: LDP works even when the routers along the way speak different languages for other things, because it is its own separate way of sharing tags.

sections.title: Requirement Level and Traffic Engineering
sections.content:
The memo states the requirement level for LDP: implementation is recommended for devices that perform MPLS forwarding along normally routed paths as determined by destination-based routing protocols.

Traffic engineering uses explicitly routed LSPs, which need not follow the normally routed path. Those can be set up by CR-LDP, a set of extensions to LDP, or by RSVP-TE, a set of extensions to RSVP. The memo says there is no consensus on which is technically superior, so administrators should choose based on their needs and situation.
sections.eli5: If a router sends normal traffic along the usual road, LDP is recommended. For special hand-picked routes there are two other choices, and neither is declared the winner.

sections.title: LDP Features in Brief
sections.content:
LDP associates a Forwarding Equivalence Class (FEC) with each label it distributes. Two LSRs that exchange FEC-label bindings are LDP peers, and they have an LDP session. Sessions run over TCP, so messages are delivered reliably and labels and state need not be refreshed periodically. A discovery mechanism finds potential peers, so operators need not configure each peer by hand.

Two distribution methods are supported. With Downstream Unsolicited, an LSR advertises bindings when it is ready to forward the FEC using MPLS. With Downstream on Demand, it provides a binding only in response to a peer's request. LSRs may use liberal or conservative label retention, and independent or ordered control for when to advertise.

LDP also defines an optional loop detection mechanism for LSPs crossing non-TTL MPLS clouds, though an LDP-compliant LSR must implement it. An extension mechanism covers vendor-private and experimental messages and TLVs.
sections.eli5: Routers become pen pals over a reliable line, then agree on how to trade tags: only when asked, or whenever they have one ready.

sections.title: Scalability
sections.content:
The memo lists factors that affect how well LDP implementations scale. Label distribution is incremental, so no periodic refresh of bindings is needed. Where labels are scarce, as on ATM and Frame Relay links, Downstream on Demand with conservative retention allocates only the labels needed for normally routed paths.

Where labels are not scarce, Downstream Unsolicited with liberal retention means a change of FEC nexthop from one peer to another needs no distribution action. Limits on the number of TCP connections limit the number of peers, and the optional path vector loop detection adds memory, processing and LDP traffic.
sections.eli5: If tags are rare, ask for only the ones you need. If tags are plentiful, collect them all so switching routes is quick.

sections.title: Security
sections.content: LDP defines optional use of the TCP MD5 Signature Option to protect against spoofed TCP segments being injected into LDP session connections. This is similar to how BGP uses the option, as specified in RFC 2385.
sections.eli5: Routers can add a secret stamp to their messages so nobody can slip in fake ones.
